records.why: The old total '12 x 40 = 480' ignored that Lessons 4 and 12 are already 80-minute double lessons. Several other lessons cannot fit their activities in 40 minutes (for example Lesson 2 has three 8-minute stations before any discussion, Lesson 6 has two 10-minute practical stations plus calculations and lenses, Lesson 9 lists 8+20+20+5+7 = 60 minutes). I chose one period length for each lesson: double (80 min) for Lessons 2, 4, 6, 8, 9, 11, 12 and single (40 min) for Lessons 1, 3, 5, 7, 10. Total = 5 x 40 + 7 x 80 = 200 + 560 = 760 minutes, which equals 19 periods of 40 minutes, matching the 19 lessons that the KICD design suggests for this sub-strand. Teacher decision: confirm that your timetable can give double periods to these seven lessons, or say which lessons should be cut or split.

records.why: The Observe phase added to 53 minutes (15 + 30 + 8), so with Predict, Explain, Driving Question Board and Model Building the lesson came to about 84 minutes in an 80-minute period; Part A is now 12 minutes and Part C 5 minutes (47 minutes of Observe). The duration line also said '40 minutes classroom + 40 minutes field', but the Explain, Driving Question Board and Model phases come after the field work. I also added a low-cost way to mark 50 m (a rope, or about 67 paces: 50 / 0.75 = 66.7) because a 50 m tape is not available in every partner school.
records.old: Part A (15 min, classroom): In groups of four, with roles (timekeeper, recorder, calculator, reporter), learners receive the echo table with distances and use t = 2d/v with v = 340 m/s to calculate the delay at each site: A 85 m gives round trip 170 m and delay 0.50 s; B 170 m gives 340 m and 1.00 s; C 12 m gives 24 m and 0.07 s; D 300 m gives 600 m and 1.76 s. They compare each delay with the 0.1 s ear limit and derive the minimum distance 0.1 x 340 / 2 = 17 m. Part B (30 min, field): The class goes to the school's long stone wall. Using the tape measure, learners mark 50 m from the wall. One learner claps and listens, and adjusts the clapping rhythm until each clap coincides with the returning echo of the previous clap. Kiprono's role is played by a timekeeper who starts the stopwatch on a clap and stops it after 10 clap-echo intervals. Groups record time for 10 intervals (class example: 2.94 s), compute one interval (0.294 s) and calculate d = 340 x 0.294 / 2 = 49.98 m, about 50 m, then compare with the tape measure value and discuss sources of error such as reaction time and wind. Part C (8 min): Learners compare the 'surface table' (cliff rock 90%, painted concrete 85%, wooden board 60%, curtains 15%, thick grass or foam mattress 10%) and optionally test by clapping near a classroom curtain, a wooden board and a foam mattress, listening for loudness of the return.
records.new: Part A (12 min, classroom): In groups of four, with roles (timekeeper, recorder, calculator, reporter), learners receive the echo table with distances and use t = 2d/v with v = 340 m/s to calculate the delay at each site: A 85 m gives round trip 170 m and delay 0.50 s; B 170 m gives 340 m and 1.00 s; C 12 m gives 24 m and 0.07 s; D 300 m gives 600 m and 1.76 s. They compare each delay with the 0.1 s ear limit and derive the minimum distance 0.1 x 340 / 2 = 17 m. Part B (30 min, field): The class goes to the school's long stone wall. Using the tape measure, learners mark 50 m from the wall (if there is no 50 m tape, use a 50 m rope or string, or pace it out: one pace is about 0.75 m, so about 67 paces; measure 10 paces with a tape first to check). One learner claps and listens, and adjusts the clapping rhythm until each clap coincides with the returning echo of the previous clap. Kiprono's role is played by a timekeeper who starts the stopwatch on a clap and stops it after 10 clap-echo intervals. Groups record time for 10 intervals (class example: 2.94 s), compute one interval (0.294 s) and calculate d = 340 x 0.294 / 2 = 49.98 m, about 50 m, then compare with the tape measure value and discuss sources of error such as reaction time and wind. Part C (5 min): Learners compare the 'surface table' (cliff rock 90%, painted concrete 85%, wooden board 60%, curtains 15%, thick grass or foam mattress 10%) and optionally test by clapping near a classroom curtain, a wooden board and a foam mattress, listening for loudness of the return.

records.value:
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) explain the wave properties in real-life situations,
b) demonstrate the properties of waves in nature,
c) demonstrate the formation and properties of stationary waves in nature,
d) describe applications of stationary waves in day-to-day life,
e) describe Doppler effect and its applications in day-to-day life,
f) appreciate formation and application of waves in real-life situations.

Where the lessons teach them: (a) and (b) Lessons 1 to 8; (c) and (d) Lesson 9; applications of wave properties, including modulation, Lesson 11; (e) Lesson 10; (f) Lessons 11 and 12.

records.why: Diffraction is the bending of waves round edges and through gaps. A shout is weaker far away on open ground because the energy spreads over a larger and larger area (the intensity falls as the area grows), not because of diffraction. Treating the two as one would teach learners a wrong cause. Checked against the standard treatments of sound intensity (energy shared over the area of a sphere, so the intensity falls with distance) and of diffraction (depends on wavelength compared with gap size).
records.old: It spreads, and that spreading helps explain why the sound is weaker in open places such as the Nairobi grounds and why it fills the Kisumu hall.
records.new: It spreads. Diffraction explains how the sound bends round edges and through gaps, such as a doorway into a corridor of the Kisumu hall. The sound also gets weaker on the open Nairobi grounds, but that is because the wave spreads out in all directions so the same energy covers a bigger area; this is a different effect from diffraction, and learners keep the two apart.
records.reference: OpenStax University Physics Volume 1, Chapter 17 (Sound), section 17.3 Sound Intensity, and Volume 3, Chapter 4 (Diffraction)
records.group_headline: Lesson 7 said diffraction explains why a shout is weak on open ground; that is ordinary spreading out of the wave, not diffraction, so the two ideas are now kept apart

records.new: and it keeps two ideas apart: diffraction (bending round edges and through gaps) and the ordinary spreading out of a shout in all directions, which weakens it on the open Nairobi grounds.
records.reference: OpenStax University Physics Volume 1, Chapter 17 (Sound), section 17.3 Sound Intensity, and Volume 3, Chapter 4 (Diffraction)

records.why: Amina walks at about 1 to 2 m/s while sound travels at 340 m/s, so the claps reaching Otieno and Wanjiru differ by less than 1 percent and learners cannot count any difference; the lesson claimed they would. A scale model fixes this: wave speed 1 m/s, source speed 0.5 m/s, clap every 1 s. Gap between wavefronts ahead = (1 - 0.5) x 1 = 0.5 m, so a wavefront arrives every 0.5 s (2 per second); behind = (1 + 0.5) x 1 = 1.5 m, so one every 1.5 s (0.67 per second). I checked it against f' = f v/(v - u) = 1 x 1/0.5 = 2 Hz and f v/(v + u) = 1/1.5 = 0.67 Hz. Teacher decision: this changes the activity design; confirm that chalk and string (or a compass on paper) are available and that you prefer this to the original walk.
records.old: First, a human-model walk-through in an open space: one learner (Amina) acts as the siren and walks steadily while clapping once per second. A second learner (Otieno) stands still ahead as the observer and a third (Wanjiru) stands behind. Other learners count claps heard per ten seconds at each position. The class sees that Otieno receives claps more often and Wanjiru less often, because each clap starts from a position closer to or further from them. Second, groups draw wavefronts from a moving source on paper: circles starting from successive positions, bunched up in front and stretched behind.
records.new: First, a scale model of the moving source in an open space. A walking learner is far too slow to change the pitch of a real clap, so the wave is slowed down: 1 m on the ground stands for 1 second of wave travel. One learner (Amina) acts as the siren and walks steadily along a chalk line at 0.5 m/s while a timekeeper claps once per second; a partner marks Amina's position at each clap. Second, groups draw the wavefronts on the ground (string and chalk) or on paper (compass): from each mark a circle whose radius is 1 m for every second since that clap, so the circles start from successive positions of the source. The circles are bunched up in front of Amina (0.5 m apart) and stretched behind her (1.5 m apart). Otieno stands ahead and Wanjiru behind, and each works out how often a wavefront reaches them: every 0.5 s for Otieno (2 per second) and every 1.5 s for Wanjiru (about 0.7 per second), compared with 1 per second if Amina stood still.
records.reference: OpenStax University Physics Volume 1, Chapter 17, section 17.7 The Doppler Effect (wave speed is set by the medium, not by the source)

records.why: A tube or cylinder with water is closed at one end, so the first resonance is at L = wavelength/4, not wavelength/2. With the 2L rule learners would expect the wrong length. Check: wavelength = 340/500 = 0.68 m; L = 0.68/4 = 0.17 m; three quarters = 0.51 m; for a 512 Hz fork 340/512/4 = 0.166 m. The same edit also moves the Observe time to about 28 minutes to match the 80-minute allocation.
records.old: (Part of 20 minutes in total for observing) Station A (PhET: Standing Waves on a String, or a phone/projector demonstration if computers are scarce): groups of 3-4 run the simulation, set the string to fixed ends, change the frequency slowly, and watch for the frequencies at which a clear stable pattern forms. They record in a table: number of loops, number of nodes (including ends), number of antinodes, and relative frequency (f, 2f, 3f). They observe that between those frequencies the pattern is messy and small. Station B (hands-on): either (i) a 3-4 m rope or elastic cord fixed at one end and shaken by hand at the other, or a 0.60 m taut string or wire on a sonometer/nyatiti; or (ii) an air column: a tube or measuring cylinder with water, a tuning fork (for example 500 Hz or 512 Hz) and the water level adjusted until the sound suddenly becomes loud (resonance). Learners mark nodes with chalk or tape and antinodes with a different mark, measure length L with a tape measure, and compare fundamental and second harmonic. They also measure the pitch change when they press the string to make it shorter (like a nyatiti player) or use a shorter tube (like covering flute holes). Kiprono times the vibrations with a stopwatch where possible, Amina draws the patterns, Otieno reads measurements, Wanjiru checks the table and asks 'Why only these frequencies?'
records.new: (about 28 minutes in total for observing) Station A (PhET: Standing Waves on a String, or a phone/projector demonstration if computers are scarce): groups of 3-4 run the simulation, set the string to fixed ends, change the frequency slowly, and watch for the frequencies at which a clear stable pattern forms. They record in a table: number of loops, number of nodes (including ends), number of antinodes, and relative frequency (f, 2f, 3f). They observe that between those frequencies the pattern is messy and small. Station B (hands-on): either (i) a 3-4 m rope or elastic cord fixed at one end and shaken by hand at the other, or a 0.60 m taut string or wire on a sonometer/nyatiti; or (ii) an air column: a tube or measuring cylinder with water, a tuning fork (for example 500 Hz or 512 Hz) and the water level adjusted until the sound suddenly becomes loud (resonance). This air column is closed at the water end, so it resonates when L is about one quarter of a wavelength (for a 500 Hz fork the wavelength is 340/500 = 0.68 m, so L is about 0.17 m, a little less because of end effects) and again at three quarters (about 0.51 m); the wavelength = 2L rule applies to a tube open at both ends, such as the flute. Learners mark nodes with chalk or tape and antinodes with a different mark, measure length L with a tape measure, and compare fundamental and second harmonic. They also measure the pitch change when they press the string to make it shorter (like a nyatiti player) or use a shorter tube (like covering flute holes). Kiprono times the vibrations with a stopwatch where possible, Amina draws the patterns, Otieno reads measurements, Wanjiru checks the table and asks 'Why only these frequencies?'
records.reference: OpenStax University Physics Volume 1, Chapter 17, section 17.4 Normal Modes of a Standing Sound Wave

records.new: (c) Sound can turn the corner of a 1.0 m doorway but a torch beam makes a sharp patch. Use the wavelength of a 340 Hz sound and the wavelength of light (5.5 x 10^-7 m) to explain this. (d) A nyatiti string is 0.60 m long and waves travel along it at 120 m/s. Find the frequency of its fundamental (lowest) stationary wave, say what a node is, and say what happens to the pitch if the player presses the string so that only 0.30 m vibrates. (e) Explain, without calculating, why an ambulance siren sounds higher as it comes towards you than after it has passed. (f) A radio station uses a carrier wave of 91.0 MHz to carry a voice. records.why: Knock-on: model answers for the new questions (d), (e) and (f). Checks: 2 x 0.60 = 1.20; 120/1.20 = 100; 120/0.60 = 200; 3.0e8/2.0e4 = 1.5e4 m.
records.old: Diffraction does not change the frequency or the wavelength.
records.new: Diffraction does not change the frequency or the wavelength. (d) Wavelength = 2L = 2 x 0.60 = 1.20 m, so f = v / wavelength = 120 / 1.20 = 100 Hz. A node is a point on the stationary wave where the amplitude is always zero, because the incident and reflected waves cancel there. If only 0.30 m vibrates, wavelength = 0.60 m and f = 120 / 0.60 = 200 Hz, a higher pitch: a shorter string gives a higher frequency. (e) The siren always gives out the same frequency. As the ambulance moves towards you, each wavefront starts closer to you than the one before, so the wavefronts are bunched up and more of them reach your ear each second: a higher frequency, which you hear as a higher pitch. After it passes, the wavefronts are stretched out, fewer arrive each second and the pitch is lower. The speed of sound does not change. (f) Audio frequencies (about 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz) as radio waves would have wavelengths of kilometres (3.0 x 10^8 / 2.0 x 10^4 = 15 000 m for 20 kHz), needing enormous aerials, and every station would use the same frequencies and mix together. A high-frequency carrier (wavelength 3.30 m at 91.0 MHz) needs a small aerial and gives each station its own frequency. In FM the voice signal changes the frequency of the carrier while its amplitude stays the same, and the receiver detects those changes and turns them back into sound.

records.why: The look-for contradicted the law of reflection: if i = 30 degrees measured from the normal then r = 30 degrees, not 60. 60 degrees is the answer only when the ray makes 30 degrees with the surface (then i = 90 - 30 = 60 and r = 60). Checked: 90 - 30 = 60; i = r.

records.why: Saying that interference makes the hall muddy is only part of the story: for speech, which has many frequencies, the muddy lingering sound is reverberation (overlap in time), while interference gives seat-to-seat differences in loudness. The note keeps learners from carrying a half-true idea into the Final Explanation.

Be precise about the hall: a voice contains many frequencies, so the muddiness comes mainly from reflections arriving one after another and overlapping in time (reverberation, Lesson 4); interference explains why some seats are louder or quieter than others, not the lingering sound itself.
